Alcmaeon of Croton

The brain hypothesis begins with Alcmaeon of Croton (c. 500 BCE), a physician-philosopher who declared that the brain, not the heart, is the seat of understanding. By tracing sensory channels (most likely the optic nerves) from the sense organs to the brain, Alcmaeon inferred that perception is a process that terminates in a central organ capable of integrating disparate signals—a claim that would not be universally accepted for another two millennia.

Democritus

Democritus (c. 460–370 BCE) offered the first thoroughgoing materialist account of perception. Objects shed thin films of atoms called eidola, which travel through the air and impinge on the sense organs, where they interact with the atomic structure of the perceiver. Mind itself is composed of fine, spherical, highly mobile atoms distributed through the body but concentrated in the brain. Every mental event—thought, sensation, emotion—is atomic motion, and nothing more.

Hippocrates

The Hippocratic text On the Sacred Disease 1 mounted a vigorous defense of the brain doctrine against cardiocentrism: “Men ought to know that from nothing else but the brain come joys, delights, laughter and sports, and sorrows, griefs, despondency, and lamentations.” By arguing that epilepsy is a brain disorder rather than a divine affliction, Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BCE) established that pathologies of experience are pathologies of the organ that produces experience.

Plato

Plato (c. 428–348 BCE) was less interested in the brain per se than in the epistemic situation of any perceiving mind. The Allegory of the Cave 2 depicts prisoners who mistake projected shadows for reality—an image that resonates strikingly with the modern view of perception as an internally generated model constrained by incomplete sensory data. In the Timaeus [Timaeus], Plato located the rational soul in the head, the spirited soul in the chest, and the appetitive soul in the abdomen, producing an early—if speculative—functional neuroanatomy.

Aristotle

Aristotle (c. 384–322 BCE) produced the most systematic ancient treatment of the mind in De Anima 3. He introduced phantasia (imagination), the faculty that produces internal images persisting after sensation ceases—a precursor to the concept of endogenous neural representation. His sensus communis (common sense) is a faculty that binds inputs from the individual senses into a unified percept, anticipating the binding problem. Ironically, Aristotle was a committed cardiocentrist who assigned the brain the role of a cooling organ for the blood, a reminder that even the most rigorous thinkers can be led astray when anatomical evidence is sparse. Empedocles

Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE) proposed that all matter is composed of four roots—earth, water, air, fire—driven by two cosmic forces: Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion) 4, 5. Perception operates through a system of pores: effluences streaming from objects enter pores of matching size and shape in the sense organs, so that “like perceives like.” Crucially, Empedocles located thought and consciousness not in the brain but in the blood around the heart—a cardiocentrist position that Aristotle would later adopt. His model of perception as structural matching between emitted patterns and receiving channels is a proto-mechanistic account that reduces representation to physical correspondence between object and organ.

Anaxagoras

Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) introduced Nous (Mind, Intellect) as a fundamental cosmic principle: the finest and purest of all substances, unmixed with the matter it organizes, which initiates and governs the rotation of the cosmos from primordial chaos [fragments; reported in Plato’s Phaedo and Aristotle’s Metaphysics]. Unlike the material elements, Nous “has knowledge of all things and the greatest power.” While later philosophers—most notably Socrates, as Plato reports him—were disappointed that Anaxagoras then used Nous merely as a mechanical trigger rather than a purposive intelligence, the concept marks a critical philosophical step: the identification of an ordering, information-processing principle ontologically distinct from the material substrate it organizes—a separation of the “program” from the “hardware” that anticipates functionalism by two and a half millennia.
